_readme: Hand-written glosses, distractors, families and teaching notes for Matthew. Generated by build-matthew-glossary.mjs — edit that, not this. 526 entries are written here; the rest are reused from the John, Mark, 1 John and Gospels glossaries. Glosses are short TEACHING meanings for a beginner reading Matthew, not lexicon entries. A Koine specialist should read all of them.

words.familyNotes: A contract verb: the stem vowel α merges with the ending.
Shares a family with ἀγαπάω, to love.
The same family gives both “cosmos” and “cosmetic”.
Shares a family with πίστις (faith) and πιστός (faithful).
words.notes: The -ω ending marks 1st person singular present; -ει marks 3rd person.
The only occurrence of this noun in the whole New Testament — a genuine hapax legomenon, in 5:4. The related verb νικάω is common; the noun is not.
Three occurrences in the New Testament, all of them in this letter (2:20, 2:27 twice). It shares its root with Χριστός, 'anointed'.
Twice in the New Testament, both here (2:2, 4:10). English has no short equivalent; 'propitiation' and 'expiation' are both attempts at it.
Three occurrences in the New Testament, two of them here in 3:15 — literally 'man-killer'.
Not ζωή. βίος is life as means and duration — the ἀλαζονεία τοῦ βίου in 2:16 is pride in what one has.
The author's word for his readers — seven of its eight New Testament occurrences are in this letter. A diminutive of τέκνον, and affectionate rather than belittling.
Walking as a way of living — the same idiom Hebrew uses. 'To walk in the light' is not a journey.

words.gloss: I have come, I am present

words.notes: Four occurrences in the New Testament. In 1:1 it is deliberately physical: what the writer's hands handled.

words.gloss: I touch, I take hold of

words.familyNotes: Suppletive: its aorist is εἶπον, from a different family altogether.
Behind γραφή (writing, Scripture) and every English -graphy.

words.notes: Twice in the New Testament, both in this letter (1:5, 3:11).

words.gloss: I beget, I give birth to
words.notes: Ten occurrences here, always in the perfect passive: those 'begotten of God'. The image is birth, not adoption.

words.gloss: I take up, I take away

words.notes: Three occurrences in the New Testament, two of them in 3:20–21 — the heart condemning its owner.
Twice in the New Testament. In 4:18 it is what perfect love casts out fear of.
Literally the entrails, which Greek treats as the seat of pity. 'Shuts up his σπλάγχνα' in 3:17 is closing off compassion.

words.familyNotes: Behind λόγος, λέγω (say) and every English -logy.
words.notes: 2nd declension. The -ος ending marks nominative singular; the accusative is λόγον.
Every attested ending here begins with omicron, so the corpus invariant looks like αἰωνιο-. The standard analysis is stem αἰωνι- with the 2nd-declension -ος ending.

Suppletive: πολύς beside πολλή and πολλῶν. Derivation produced a one-letter stem, which is no morpheme at all. The Attic course dropped this word rather than assert πολ-, because there it collided with πόλις; 1 John has no πόλις, so the split is stated here with that reasoning on the record.

Unaccented and enclitic. Its accented twin τίς is the question word — the accent is the only thing that separates 'someone' from 'who?', which is why ids here cannot be generated from the letters alone.
Mark's signature word — twenty occurrences in four chapters. It drives the narrative: things happen at once, and then at once again.

words.gloss: I am beside myself, I amaze
I mend, I put in order
it is a care to, it matters
I go through, I cross over
I throw on, I beat upon

words.notes: Ten occurrences, most of them in the parable of the sower, where γῆ is the ground a seed falls on rather than the world.

words.gloss: I unroof, I remove the roof
I stand by, I am present
I am possessed by a demon
I convulse, I throw into spasms
I cast out, I drive out

words.notes: Same root as ἀπαγγέλλω 'I announce' — an ἄγγελος is one who brings a message, and the theological sense is downstream of that. English 'angel' and 'evangel' are the same word twice.
No morpheme is marked: a possessive pronoun with no separable stem worth highlighting.

words.gloss: I summon, I call to myself

words.notes: MorphGNT writes the movable ν in literal parentheses — ἔξεστι(ν) — so the lemma contains characters that are not letters and no letter index can be marked on it.

words.gloss: I search out, I hunt down
I fall upon, I press on
I am strong, I am able
a householder, a master of a house
I am weak, I am sick
I come to an end, I die
I take away, I cut off
I keep watch, I stay awake
a prison; a watch of the night
I curse, I bind with an oath
a place, a piece of land
I do not know, I am ignorant
I complete, I bring to an end
I abound, I have more than enough
I go before, I lead the way
I go about, I travel around
I lead up, I bring up

words.notes: βίβλος γενέσεως — 'the book of the genesis of Jesus Christ'. The same phrase opens the genealogies of Genesis in the Greek Old Testament, which is the point.
The first of four women in a genealogy that otherwise names only fathers. Her story is Genesis 38, and it is not a decorous one.
The Boaz of the Ruth track, four verses into a Greek gospel. Matthew spells him Βόες; the Septuagint of Ruth has Βοος.
The Moabitess of the Hebrew track, named here as David's great-grandmother — which is what the book of Ruth spends four chapters getting to.
Bathsheba is not named — she is 'the wife of Uriah'. Matthew keeps the accusation in the genealogy.
The hinge of the genealogy: Matthew counts fourteen generations to David, fourteen to the deportation, fourteen from it. The exile is treated as an event on the scale of the monarchy itself.
1:19 — Joseph, unwilling to δειγματίσαι her, resolves to divorce her quietly. The word is about making an example of someone in public.
Indeclinable, and always in the phrase κατ' ὄναρ, 'in a dream'. Five times in Matthew and nowhere else in the New Testament — every warning in the infancy narrative arrives this way.
Persian court astrologers, not kings and not necessarily three — Matthew never counts them. 'Wise men' is a translator's softening.

words.gloss: I am warned, I am instructed (by God)
I kill, I do away with

words.notes: Seven times, and six of those in the formula κλαυθμὸς καὶ ὁ βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων — 'weeping and gnashing of teeth', which is Matthew's own refrain for exclusion from the kingdom.
Literally 'moonstruck' — the ancient name for the falling sickness, from the belief that the moon caused it. Rendered 'lunatic' in older English for exactly the same reason.
Not weakness. The word is used of a horse broken to the bridle — strength under control.

words.gloss: I become tasteless, I make foolish

words.notes: 5:18 — not one ἰῶτα or κεραία will pass from the law. The iota stands for the Hebrew yod, the smallest letter in the alphabet.
Left untranslated by Matthew himself. Roughly 'empty-head' — contemptuous, but the point of the saying is that the insult is treated as a capital matter.

words.gloss: an accuser, an opponent at law

words.notes: Matthew's characteristic phrase is ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ οὐράνιος, 'your heavenly Father' — where Mark and Luke more often say simply 'God'.

words.gloss: I babble, I heap up empty words
I am heard, I listen to

words.notes: The hardest word in the Lord's Prayer. It occurs nowhere else in Greek literature before this, so 'daily' is a reasoned guess rather than a translation.

words.gloss: I bring into, I lead into

words.notes: A mud-brick wall is dug through rather than forced. The thief in 6:19 does not pick a lock; he makes a hole.

words.gloss: I despise, I think little of

words.notes: An Aramaic word for property or wealth, left untranslated. Matthew treats it as the name of a rival master, not merely as money.
Matthew's own word — four of its five New Testament occurrences are here. It is a rebuke to disciples, never to outsiders.

words.gloss: I found, I lay a foundation

words.notes: 9:13 and 12:7 both quote Hosea: ἔλεος θέλω καὶ οὐ θυσίαν, 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice'. Only Matthew uses the line, and he uses it twice.

words.gloss: I have a flow of blood
I call by a name, I nickname
I set at variance, I divide
Hades, the realm of the dead

words.notes: The 'sign of Jonah' — three days in the fish read as three days in the earth. The Hebrew track teaches the book itself.

words.gloss: a sea creature, a great fish
I stand empty, I am unoccupied
I put in order, I adorn
I grow dull, I become fat

words.notes: A specific weed that looks like wheat until it heads — which is why the parable's servants are told to wait rather than pull it. 'Tares' in older English.

words.gloss: I sow on top of, I oversow
together with, at the same time
I hide inside, I mix in

words.notes: Always in συντέλεια τοῦ αἰῶνος, 'the end of the age'. The phrase is Matthew's — it is how the book closes, in 28:20.

words.gloss: I make a disciple, I am discipled
words.notes: The verb of the Great Commission — μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, 'make disciples of all nations' (28:19). It is a Matthean word.

words.gloss: I put away, I lay aside
I bring safely through, I heal

words.notes: 16:22 — Peter's ἵλεώς σοι, κύριε is an idiom of protest: 'may God be merciful to you', that is, 'this must never happen to you'.

Roughly six thousand denarii — some twenty years of a labourer's wages. Ten thousand of them is a deliberately unpayable number, and the joke of the parable is that the same man then throttles a colleague over a hundred.

words.gloss: because of, for the sake of
I am joined to, I cling
an eye (of a needle), a hole

words.notes: Matthew uses it three times and every one is edged — to the grumbling labourer, to the guest with no wedding garment, and to Judas in the garden. 'Friend' is not warmth here.

words.gloss: a donkey, a beast of burden
I change my mind, I regret
I crush, I scatter like chaff
I neglect, I pay no attention
I tithe, I give a tenth

words.notes: Matthew normally writes Ἱεροσόλυμα, the Greek-shaped form. He switches to the indeclinable Hebrew Ἰερουσαλήμ for the lament in 23:37 — the vocative of a city being mourned.

words.gloss: I appoint, I put in charge
I delay, I take a long time

words.notes: 26:18 — 'go into the city to ὁ δεῖνα'. Greek's placeholder for a name the speaker will not or need not give, like English 'such a one'.

words.gloss: I draw out, I pull away
I put under oath, I adjure
I curse, I call down a curse

words.notes: 27:46, left in Aramaic and then translated by Matthew himself. It is the opening of Psalm 22, and the bystanders mishear it as a call for Elijah.
A Latin loanword, custodia, in Greek dress — one of several signs that Matthew's world is an occupied one.
